before.content_html:
What Is the United Kingdom?

The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland is made up of four nations: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Each nation has its own distinct culture, language traditions, history and, in some cases, its own devolved government. Scotland has the Scottish Parliament, Wales has the Senedd (the Welsh Parliament) and Northern Ireland has the Northern Ireland Assembly. England does not have its own separate parliament; matters affecting only England are generally decided by the UK Parliament at Westminster. This four-nation structure means that questions of national identity are especially complex in the UK: someone may identify simultaneously as Welsh, British and European — a phenomenon known as multiple identities.

Key Fact

The UK consists of England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland each have their own devolved legislature (Scottish Parliament, Senedd and Northern Ireland Assembly). England does not have a separate parliament.

What Shapes Our Identities?

Identity is shaped by a wide range of factors operating at different levels. At the individual level, a person’s sense of self is influenced by family background, religion, language, ethnicity, gender, class and personal experience. At the group level, people form shared identities through membership of communities — a faith community, a sports club, a neighbourhood, a professional group. At the national level, institutions such as Parliament, the NHS and the legal system, as well as shared historical events and cultural traditions, contribute to a sense of belonging to the UK. At the global level, shared religion, language communities (such as the Commonwealth) and shared global causes also form part of many people’s identity.

Importantly, identity is not fixed. It shifts over time as people’s circumstances, relationships and experiences change. A teenager living in Cardiff might feel strongly Welsh, British and European all at once; the same person at a different stage of life might place different emphasis on different aspects of their identity. Citizenship studies recognise that this fluidity is normal and that having multiple identities does not mean there is any conflict between them.

The Diverse Nature of the UK Population

The UK has a long history of diversity. Over centuries, waves of migration have brought people from across Europe, Asia, Africa, the Caribbean and beyond, each contributing to the cultural, economic and social fabric of the country. According to the 2021 Census for England and Wales, about 26% of the population described themselves as belonging to an ethnic group other than White British. The UK is also religiously diverse: Christianity remains the most commonly stated religion, but significant communities practise Islam, Hinduism, Sikhism, Judaism and Buddhism, alongside a growing proportion of people who identify as having no religion.

Diversity in the UK encompasses not only ethnicity and religion but also language (over 300 languages are spoken in London alone), age, disability, sexual orientation and gender identity. The Equality Act 2010 protects nine “protected characteristics” in law: age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, and sexual orientation.

Key Fact

The Equality Act 2010 lists nine protected characteristics: age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, and sexual orientation. Discrimination on any of these grounds is unlawful.

Mutual Respect and Understanding

Mutual respect is one of the core values of British civic life. It means recognising that other people have the right to hold different beliefs, follow different cultural practices and live differently, as long as they do not harm others or breach the law. In practice, mutual respect is embedded in laws against hate crime, in equality legislation and in public sector duties to promote equality of opportunity.

The democratic values that underpin British society — the rule of law, individual liberty and democratic participation — depend on mutual respect to function. If citizens refuse to accept the legitimacy of others’ participation in public life, democratic institutions are weakened. Schools, courts, local councils and community organisations all play a role in promoting understanding and building social cohesion.

Supporters of multiculturalism argue that diversity strengthens society: different cultural perspectives foster creativity, economic dynamism and cultural exchange. They point to examples of communities that have enriched British life — in art, food, sport, science and public service — and argue that celebrating cultural difference is more honest and inclusive than expecting all citizens to adopt a single dominant cultural identity. They argue that the Equality Act 2010 and the Human Rights Act 1998 provide the legal framework needed to protect individuals while sustaining diversity.

Critics of multiculturalism argue that if too much emphasis is placed on group identities and cultural differences, it can make it harder to build the shared civic values needed for a cohesive society. Some argue that a stronger emphasis on a single, shared national identity would reduce social fragmentation and help everyone feel they belong. Others point to specific policy debates — for example, around language education for new arrivals, or the teaching of shared history in schools — as areas where a lack of common ground can create tension. Examiners expect students to present both viewpoints without endorsing either as the correct answer.

Some students assume that a person who identifies strongly with their ethnic heritage, religion or regional background is somehow less committed to being British. Citizenship studies reject this assumption. Multiple identities are the norm for most people: a person can feel deeply proud of their Scottish heritage, their Muslim faith and their British citizenship all at once. These identities reinforce rather than compete with one another in most people’s experience. The concept of multiple identities is explicitly taught in the specification precisely because it reflects the reality of life in the contemporary UK.

Why Diversity Matters for Democracy

A diverse society is not without challenges. Discrimination, prejudice and hate crime remain real problems that the law seeks to address. At the same time, diversity is also a strength: exposure to different perspectives can improve decision-making, challenge assumptions and produce more creative solutions to shared problems. A democracy that genuinely represents all its citizens — including those from minority ethnic backgrounds, different faiths, and all regions of the UK — is more likely to make decisions that are fair and sustainable in the long run.

What Does It Mean to Live in British Society?

Every society is built on a shared set of values — ideas about how people should treat one another and how public life should be organised. In the United Kingdom, these values have developed over centuries through law, tradition and democratic debate. Understanding them is not just an academic exercise; they shape the rights you hold, the duties you owe and the freedoms you enjoy as a citizen.

The Key Principles Underpinning British Society

Four principles are commonly identified as the foundation of British civic life. First, democracy means that citizens choose who governs them and can remove governments they no longer support. Second, the rule of law means that laws apply equally to all people — no individual or institution is above them. Third, individual liberty protects personal freedoms such as freedom of speech, freedom of conscience and freedom of movement within the limits set by law. Fourth, mutual respect and tolerance of those with different faiths and beliefs underpins peaceful coexistence in a diverse society.

Key Fact

The four key principles underpinning British society are: democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty, and mutual respect and tolerance for those with different faiths and beliefs.

Rights, Duties and Freedoms

Citizens in the UK hold a range of rights and freedoms. Human rights are protections that apply to every person. The Human Rights Act 1998 brought the European Convention on Human Rights into UK domestic law, meaning these rights can be enforced in British courts. Examples include the right to a fair trial, the right to free speech and the right to privacy.

Alongside rights come legal duties — obligations set out in law that citizens must fulfil. These include paying taxes, obeying the law, and serving on a jury if summoned. Beyond legal duties, many argue that citizens also have broader moral responsibilities: voting in elections, volunteering in their communities and treating others with fairness.

Equalities are protected by legislation such as the Equality Act 2010, which makes it unlawful to discriminate against people on the basis of protected characteristics including age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, and sexual orientation. The principle of equality before the law means that the same rules apply regardless of a person’s background or identity.

Many students assume that rights are unlimited — that if you have a right, no one can ever interfere with it. This is only true of a small number of “absolute rights” (such as freedom from torture, which can never be removed under any circumstances). Most rights are “qualified rights” or “limited rights”. Freedom of expression, for example, is qualified: it can be lawfully restricted to protect national security, prevent disorder, or safeguard the reputation of others. The key point is that any restriction must be lawful, necessary and proportionate.

Rights are balanced against the rights of others. Your right to free speech does not give you the right to incite hatred against another person. Your right to protest does not override another person’s right to go about their daily life without harassment. Citizenship examiners frequently test this “balancing” idea in extended-response questions.

Moral, Legal and Political Rights

It is useful to distinguish three types of rights. Moral rights are rooted in shared ethical beliefs — for example, many people believe every child has a moral right to an education, even in countries where that right is not legally guaranteed. Legal rights are rights that are enforceable in a court of law, created by legislation or established through case law. Political rights relate specifically to participation in public life: the right to vote, to stand for election, to join a political party, and to take part in free and fair elections.

Key Fact

Moral rights are ethical claims not always in law; legal rights are enforceable in court; political rights cover participation in democracy, including voting and standing for election.

What Creates Identity?

Values and principles do not exist in a vacuum; they are shaped by — and help shape — identity. At an individual level, identity is shaped by factors such as family background, religion, language, ethnicity, gender, class and personal experience. At a group level, communities form shared identities around shared interests, heritage or beliefs. At a national level, a sense of belonging to the UK as a whole is shaped by shared institutions (Parliament, the NHS, the legal system), shared history and shared values. At a global level, many people also feel part of wider communities defined by religion, language or shared causes such as environmentalism.

Supporters of promoting British values argue that democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty and mutual respect are genuinely universal civic principles that bind the diverse population of the UK together. They argue that teaching these values in schools and public life helps new arrivals integrate and gives all citizens a shared foundation on which to build a cohesive society. Organisations such as the Association for Citizenship Teaching highlight that these principles support participation in democracy and protect minority rights.

Critics argue that framing these principles specifically as “British values” risks implying that other nations or cultures do not hold them, which can come across as culturally arrogant. Some scholars and community groups argue that the label can be used to single out particular communities — especially Muslim communities — for scrutiny in ways that are not applied equally to other groups. A further critique is that the values themselves were not developed by consensus but were defined by government, and that the communities most likely to be monitored under related policies had little input into that process. Examiners expect students to present both perspectives fairly rather than endorsing either.

Duties and Responsibilities of Citizens

Rights are only sustainable when citizens also fulfil their responsibilities. Legally, this includes complying with the law and paying taxes. Morally, many argue it includes engaging with democracy: voting in local and national elections, staying informed about public issues, and holding those in power to account. Active citizenship — getting involved in communities, volunteering, campaigning on issues of public concern — is encouraged as an expression of democratic values. The balance between individual freedoms and social responsibilities is one of the central tensions in citizenship debates.

Beyond the Ballot Box

Voting in elections is the most visible way citizens participate in democracy, but it happens only once every few years. Between elections, citizens can still influence policy and hold decision-makers to account through pressure groups, trade unions, charities and other civil society organisations. Understanding how these bodies operate — and how they differ from political parties — is essential for understanding how power really works in the UK.

Pressure Groups: Inside and Outside

Pressure groups are organisations that seek to influence the policies of government and other decision-makers on behalf of their members or a particular cause. A key distinction is between insider groups and outsider groups.

Insider groups are consulted directly by government. The British Medical Association (BMA) is an example: it is regularly invited to advise on healthcare policy because its members have specialist expertise. The National Farmers’ Union advises on rural and agricultural policy. Their influence comes from credibility and established relationships, not from public protest.

Outsider groups operate differently. They do not have formal access to government and rely instead on lobbying, public demonstrations, petitions and media campaigns to put pressure on decision-makers from the outside. Outsider groups may campaign on issues ranging from animal welfare to veterans’ housing to disability rights.

A very common error is to treat pressure groups and political parties as the same because both campaign on issues. They are fundamentally different. A political party seeks to form a government by winning elections and fielding candidates across the country. A pressure group focuses on a single issue or a set of related issues and does not aim to govern. The Green Party is a political party; an environmental campaign group that lobbies MPs to legislate on plastic pollution is a pressure group. They may share some goals but their methods and ambitions are distinct.

Trade Unions: Voice in the Workplace

Trade unions are a distinctive form of collective organisation that gives working people a voice. Rather than campaigning on a single political issue, unions represent their members’ interests in the workplace: negotiating pay and working conditions, supporting members who face dismissal or unfair treatment, and advocating for wider employment rights. The Trades Union Congress (TUC) is the national body that brings together most UK trade unions.

Key Fact

Trade unions negotiate with employers through collective bargaining — where the union speaks on behalf of all its members rather than each worker negotiating individually. Unions argue this gives workers more power in disputes with employers. The TUC is the national umbrella body for UK trade unions.

Views on trade unions differ. Supporters argue that unions protect vulnerable workers, have historically won important rights (such as the minimum wage, safety regulations and maternity leave), and provide a democratic counterbalance to the power of employers. Critics argue that industrial action, including strikes, can harm public services and the wider economy, and that union power may slow business growth or job creation. Both viewpoints are part of a long-running democratic debate about the balance between workers’ rights and economic efficiency.

Charities and Voluntary Groups

Charities and voluntary organisations are part of civil society — the broad range of groups and associations that exist between government and the individual. They provide direct support to communities (food banks, mental health services, youth clubs) and often advocate for policy change on behalf of the groups they serve.

Well-known examples include Citizens Advice, which helps people with legal and financial problems; Age UK, which advocates for the elderly; and Shelter, which campaigns on housing. These organisations combine service delivery with policy advocacy, giving voice to groups who may otherwise struggle to be heard by government.

Key Fact

Civil society organisations give citizens a voice in several ways: direct advocacy to MPs and ministers; public campaigns to shape public opinion; providing evidence and expertise to parliamentary committees; running services that demonstrate unmet need. They differ from political parties in that they do not seek to form a government.

Tactics Used to Influence Policy

Pressure groups, unions and charities use a range of tactics to influence decision-makers. These include writing to MPs and ministers, presenting evidence to parliamentary select committees, organising demonstrations and marches, running media campaigns, using social media to mobilise supporters, and commissioning research to build the evidence base for their cause. The choice of tactic often depends on whether the group has insider or outsider status.

When evaluating whether pressure groups are effective, examiners want you to consider multiple factors. Insider groups tend to be more directly influential because they have formal access to government, but this access can also mean they compromise their goals in exchange for inclusion. Outsider groups rely on public opinion and media coverage, which can be powerful — a well-organised campaign with broad public support can force a government to act — but can also be unpredictable and slow.

Size and resources matter: a large organisation with many members and funding can mount a sustained campaign; a small grassroots group may struggle to maintain momentum. The political climate also matters: governments that are already sympathetic to a cause are more likely to act on pressure group demands than those that are opposed. A balanced evaluative answer will weigh these factors against each other rather than simply listing them.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Pressure groups seek to influence government policy on a specific issue without seeking to govern; political parties seek to form a government by winning elections — this is a key distinction examiners test.
  • Insider groups have direct access to policymakers and influence through consultation; outsider groups rely on lobbying, demonstrations and public campaigns.
  • Trade unions, charities and voluntary organisations are all part of civil society — they give citizens a voice between elections and provide expertise, advocacy and services that government alone cannot.

before.content_html:
Why Case Studies Matter

The specification asks you to know two contrasting examples of how citizens working together have attempted to change or improve their communities. These examples should demonstrate different methods and different contexts, so that you can compare and evaluate how citizens use collective action to address public policy, challenge injustice or resolve a community issue. Citizenship action can be local, national or international, and can focus on issues from across the political spectrum.

This lesson examines two case studies: first, the Hillsborough families’ campaign for justice; second, the campaign by disability rights organisations that contributed to the Equality Act 2010. Both are factual accounts of civic action and its outcomes, presented as models of how citizens can make a difference through sustained, organised effort.

Case Study 1: The Hillsborough Families’ Campaign

The 15 April 1989 crush at Hillsborough football stadium in Sheffield during an FA Cup semi-final caused 96 deaths. A ninety-seventh victim died in 2021. The initial official narrative wrongly blamed supporters for the disaster. Families of those who died refused to accept this account and began a campaign for the truth and legal accountability.

The Hillsborough Family Support Group used a wide range of methods over more than three decades. They petitioned Parliament, gathered and preserved evidence, engaged solicitors and barristers, lobbied MPs and successive governments, and worked with journalists to keep the issue in the public eye. In 2012, the Hillsborough Independent Panel published a report revealing failures by the authorities and alterations to police statements.

Key Fact

The Hillsborough families used petitions, legal action, lobbying, media engagement and sustained public campaigning over more than 30 years. Key outcomes: the 2012 Independent Panel report revealed failures by the authorities; later in 2012 the original inquest verdicts were quashed; in 2016 a new inquest jury returned unlawful killing verdicts for 96 victims.

The Hillsborough case illustrates several important citizenship principles. First, that ordinary citizens without formal political power can challenge state institutions and achieve justice through sustained, evidence-based campaigning. Second, that legal processes (inquests, judicial review, criminal investigation) are an important route alongside political pressure. Third, that the campaign required decades of perseverance and that meaningful change in complex cases takes time.

Case Study 2: Disability Rights and the Equality Act 2010

The Equality Act 2010 is a landmark piece of legislation that consolidated and strengthened protections against discrimination in the UK. It brought together previous laws on sex, race and disability discrimination and extended protection to nine protected characteristics. Its passage was shaped by decades of campaigning by disability rights organisations, women’s groups and equality bodies.

Disability rights organisations such as Scope and the Disability Rights Commission campaigned throughout the 1990s and 2000s for stronger legal protections. Their methods included direct advocacy to MPs and ministers, evidence submissions to parliamentary committees, public awareness campaigns, and legal challenges under existing equality legislation to test and extend its boundaries. The Disability Discrimination Act 1995 was an early result; the Equality Act 2010 consolidated and strengthened those rights further.

Key Fact

The Equality Act 2010 covers nine protected characteristics: age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, and sexual orientation. It applies to employment, education, housing and the provision of services.

This case study illustrates a different model of citizenship action. Rather than responding to a single injustice (as the Hillsborough families did), disability rights organisations pursued a long-term legislative strategy across multiple parliaments and governments. They combined insider tactics (formal consultations, committee evidence, working with sympathetic MPs) with outsider tactics (public campaigns and demonstrations), demonstrating that the two approaches are not mutually exclusive.

The Hillsborough and disability rights campaigns differ in several important ways. The Hillsborough campaign focused on a single specific injustice and pursued legal justice through the courts and inquests alongside political lobbying. The disability rights campaign pursued systemic legislative change across a wider range of issues and over a longer strategic timeline.

Both campaigns, however, share important features: they involved citizens working collectively rather than individually; they combined multiple methods (legal, political, media, public); they required persistence over years or decades; and they achieved tangible, lasting changes (the 2016 inquest verdicts; the Equality Act 2010). Both demonstrate that citizens can achieve meaningful outcomes even against powerful institutions, provided they are organised, evidence-based and persistent.

Evaluating Citizenship Actions

When you are asked to evaluate a citizenship action in the exam, you need to assess both process and outcome. Did the action achieve its stated aim? If not fully, did it make progress? Were the methods used appropriate and effective? What were the limitations or unintended consequences? A strong evaluation will consider impact from multiple perspectives — the citizens who took action, those the action was meant to help, and the wider democratic system.

Students often evaluate citizenship actions in binary terms — either “it worked” or “it failed”. Exam mark schemes reward more nuanced thinking. A campaign can partially succeed: it may change public awareness without changing law; it may change law without changing behaviour; it may achieve its immediate aim but reveal deeper structural problems. Strong evaluative answers assess what was achieved, what was not, and why — considering factors such as the resources available to the campaign, the political climate at the time, and whether the methods chosen matched the aims.

What Is a Citizenship Action Investigation?

The citizenship action investigation is a core part of the GCSE qualification. You are required to plan and carry out a citizenship action — a real, out-of-classroom activity that applies the knowledge and skills you have developed during the course. The investigation is then assessed through questions in the active citizenship section, where you describe what you did, what happened, and how effective your action was. It accounts for 15 per cent of your total GCSE marks.

A citizenship action can be local, national or international in focus. It might address a community issue (improving a local park, tackling litter on a school road), a rights-based question (raising awareness of disability access, campaigning for fair treatment of a group), a political question (engaging with local government on a public matter), or a broader social concern (food waste, youth mental health, veterans’ housing). What matters is that the issue arises from the specification content and that the action is aimed at delivering a benefit or change for others — not just for yourself.

Stage 1: Choosing the Issue

The first stage is identifying the issue you want to address. The issue must arise from the specification content, so it must connect to citizenship themes such as democracy, rights, equality, community or public services. It should be specific enough that you can take a focused action — examiners consistently reward actions that are tightly defined and locally grounded because these make evaluation easier and more meaningful.

A common mistake at this stage is choosing an issue that is too broad or too vague. “Save the environment” or “stop all crime” are not workable citizenship action issues. A better framing would be: “Reduce the amount of single-use plastic packaging sold in our school canteen”, or “Improve lighting on the path between school and the local bus stop to improve safety for students”. Specific, focused issues allow you to take concrete action and evaluate your impact clearly.

Stage 2: Research Using Primary and Secondary Sources

Before taking action, you need to understand the issue thoroughly. This means gathering evidence using both primary sources and secondary sources.

Primary research might include: conducting a survey of students or local residents about the issue; interviewing a local councillor, MP, headteacher or relevant expert; attending a public meeting or council session; or gathering your own observations and data (e.g. counting the number of cars that ignore a pedestrian crossing). Secondary research might include: reading local newspaper reports, ONS statistics, charity reports, parliamentary debate records, or academic studies on the issue.

Key Fact

Primary sources are gathered first-hand (surveys you conduct, interviews you carry out, meetings you attend). Secondary sources are produced by others (reports, statistics, newspaper articles, government publications). Strong investigations use both: primary sources show what those directly affected think and experience; secondary sources provide context, background and comparison with other places or times.

Stage 3: Planning the Action

Once you understand the issue, you plan what action to take. This should flow directly from your research: the evidence you have gathered should show why the action is needed, who the action is aimed at, and how the action addresses the issue. A good plan will include:

  • A clear aim: what change do you want to bring about?
  • The method: what will you actually do? (e.g. present a petition to the school council, write to your local MP, run a public awareness campaign, volunteer with a relevant organisation, establish a group)
  • Who you will work with: most effective citizenship actions involve collaboration with others
  • A realistic timeline and any resources or permissions needed
  • How you will measure whether the action has worked

Citizenship actions can take many different forms. Examples that span a range of issues include: letter writing to a councillor about a local park being closed (community issue); creating an e-petition on the Parliament website about access to youth mental health services (rights issue); running a volunteering programme with a local food bank to reduce food waste (social issue); organising a community litter-pick and then presenting findings to a local council meeting (environmental and civic issue); advocating for better access to facilities for disabled students in a school (equality issue).

Notice that these examples span the political spectrum — some focus on environmental concerns, others on social justice, others on community safety or resource allocation. Citizenship action is not the property of any one political viewpoint. All citizens, regardless of their political beliefs, can find issues they care about and take meaningful action.

Stages 4 and 5: Taking the Action and Assessing Impact

Stage 4 is taking the action itself. This is the practical phase: delivering your petition, sending your letters, running your campaign, attending the meeting, carrying out your volunteering. It is important to keep a record of what you actually did, including any evidence (photographs, copies of letters, notes from meetings, survey data) and any responses you received.

Stage 5 is assessing impact: did your action make a difference? Evaluation requires honesty — not all actions achieve their intended aim, and recognising this (and explaining why) is itself good citizenship thinking. Did the council respond to your petition? Did the school change its policy? Did awareness of the issue increase? How do you know?

Key Fact

The six stages: (1) Decide the question or issue; (2) Carry out initial research using primary and secondary sources; (3) Plan the action; (4) Take the action; (5) Assess the impact; (6) Evaluate the whole process. In the assessment, you will be asked about your own investigation — examiners reward answers where you name the issue, method and impact specifically, not vaguely.

Stage 6: Evaluating the Whole Process

The final stage is reflecting on the whole investigation. This is different from assessing impact (stage 5): evaluation asks the deeper question — if you did this again, what would you do differently, and why? Was your initial research thorough enough? Did you choose the most effective method? Were there obstacles you did not anticipate? What have you learned about how change happens in your community or society?

Examiner reports consistently note that students who describe a tightly focused, locally based action evaluate their impact far more successfully than those who describe broad, vague actions. “We raised awareness of climate change in our school” is difficult to evaluate because the aim is undefined and the outcome unmeasurable. “We petitioned the school canteen to remove single-use plastic drink pouches, and by June 20 per cent of the canteen’s drinks were sold in reusable bottles” gives a specific aim, a specific method, and a measurable outcome. The more specific your action and aim, the stronger your evaluation can be.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A citizenship action investigation follows six stages: choose an issue, research it using primary and secondary sources, plan the action, take the action, assess the impact, and evaluate the whole process.
  • Tightly focused, specific issues make for much stronger evaluations than broad or vague ones — examiners reward answers that name the issue, method and outcome precisely.
  • Evaluation means honest reflection on what worked, what did not, and what you would do differently — it is not the same as just describing what you did.

before.content_html:
Why Voting Systems Matter

The way votes are counted determines who governs. Different voting systems can produce very different outcomes from the same set of votes. The UK uses several voting systems for different elections: First Past the Post (FPTP) for Westminster general elections, and various forms of proportional representation for devolved elections and some local elections. Understanding the strengths and weaknesses of each system is a key citizenship skill.

First Past the Post (FPTP)

Under FPTP, the UK is divided into parliamentary constituencies. Each constituency elects one MP. Voters mark a cross next to their preferred candidate. The candidate with the most votes wins — they do not need a majority of votes, just more than anyone else. Westminster general elections use this system for all 650 seats.

Key Fact

Under FPTP, each constituency elects one MP — the candidate with the most votes wins, regardless of whether they have a majority. This is called a plurality. Westminster general elections usually take place every five years under this system.

Strengths of FPTP

Supporters of FPTP highlight several advantages. First, it usually produces a clear result: one party typically wins enough seats to form a majority government with a strong mandate to govern. Strong majority governments can implement their manifesto commitments without being blocked by coalition partners. Second, each MP represents a specific constituency, creating a direct link between voters and their elected representative. Third, the system is simple to understand and quick to count: voters mark one cross, results are declared overnight.

Supporters also argue that FPTP produces stability: governments tend to last a full term rather than collapsing when coalition partners fall out. The 2010–2015 coalition, though stable by comparative standards, showed the complexity of coalition negotiation that more proportional systems often require.

Weaknesses of FPTP

Critics of FPTP point to several serious problems. First, the system can produce large majorities from a minority of votes: a party can win a landslide majority in Parliament while winning well under half of the votes cast nationally, because votes for losing candidates in each constituency contribute nothing to the final seat count. Second, many votes are effectively “wasted” — in safe seats, the outcome is predictable regardless of the local vote, reducing the incentive to vote. Third, smaller parties that attract votes spread evenly across constituencies may win very few seats even with significant national support, meaning proportionality is low.

A very common exam error is to list FPTP advantages and disadvantages on one side, and proportional representation advantages and disadvantages on the other side, without comparing the two against each other. Examiners want explicit comparison and a substantiated judgement — for example: “While FPTP produces stable majority governments more reliably than PR, it does so at the cost of proportionality, which means millions of voters are effectively unrepresented. On balance, the gain in stability may or may not outweigh this democratic deficit depending on the criteria used.” A side-by-side list without explicit comparison and a conclusion will not reach the top band.

Proportional Representation Systems

Several forms of proportional representation (PR) are used in UK elections. These systems aim to ensure that parties win seats in rough proportion to their share of the vote, giving smaller parties and minority views better representation.

The Additional Member System (AMS) is used for elections to the Scottish Parliament. Voters cast two votes: one for a constituency MP (using FPTP) and one for a regional party list. The regional seats are allocated to correct for the disproportionality of the constituency results, producing an overall result closer to the share of the vote. The Scottish Parliament was designed to make single-party majority government difficult, encouraging coalition or minority government.

The Single Transferable Vote (STV) is used for Northern Ireland Assembly elections and Scottish local government elections. Voters rank candidates 1, 2, 3, and so on. Votes are transferred according to these preferences until all seats are filled. STV produces highly proportional results and gives voters more choice, but is complex to count and can produce results that are harder for voters to understand immediately.

Key Fact

The Additional Member System is used for Scottish Parliament elections. The Single Transferable Vote is used for Northern Ireland Assembly elections. Both produce more proportional outcomes than FPTP.

Strengths and Weaknesses of PR

Supporters of proportional systems argue that they better represent the range of views in society. Smaller parties can win seats, reducing “wasted votes” and encouraging more people to vote because their vote is more likely to count. Coalitions, which PR tends to produce, can also represent a broader range of voters’ priorities.

Critics argue that PR produces weak governments: coalition partners may disagree, making it harder to implement a clear programme, and voters may not know which parties will form a government after the election. The relationship between individual voters and a specific representative can also be weakened when large multi-member constituencies replace single-member ones. There is no consensus in the UK about which system is best: this remains a contested political question on which different parties hold different positions.

In 2011, a UK-wide referendum was held on whether to replace FPTP for Westminster elections with the Alternative Vote (AV) system, in which voters rank candidates in order of preference and the lowest-placed candidate is eliminated in successive rounds until one candidate has more than half the votes. The proposal was rejected: 67.9% voted to keep FPTP and 32.1% voted for AV. The result showed that, at that point, a majority of UK voters preferred to keep the existing system. Supporters of reform argued the question was poorly framed and that AV was not a fully proportional system in any case. The debate about electoral reform continues, with supporters of more proportional systems arguing the 2011 referendum settled only the question of AV, not the broader principle of proportional representation.

Politics in the Digital Age

For most of British history, taking part in politics meant turning up in person — to a public meeting, a polling station or a protest march. Today, citizens can sign a petition, contact their MP, or share a campaign video without leaving their homes. Digital democracy describes how the internet and social media are reshaping the ways citizens engage with government and hold it to account.

This shift raises important questions. Does digital participation make democracy more inclusive, or does it risk concentrating political voice among those who are most connected? Understanding the advantages and limits of digital civic participation is central to evaluating how healthy British democracy is today.

E-Petitions: A Route to Parliament

One of the most widely used digital tools is the e-petition. The UK Parliament’s official petition website allows any UK resident to create or sign a petition. Once a petition reaches 10,000 signatures, the government must respond formally. If it reaches 100,000 signatures, Parliament must consider holding a debate on the issue.

Key Fact

On the UK Parliament petition website: 10,000 signatures = mandatory government response; 100,000 signatures = Parliament must consider a debate. This gives ordinary citizens a direct, low-barrier route to put an issue on the parliamentary agenda.

E-petitions have been used on a wide range of issues — from animal welfare to veterans’ housing, from road safety to climate policy. They are non-partisan: a petition calling for tougher sentences for rural crime attracts signatories from across the political spectrum, as does one calling for greater investment in mental health services. The key democratic value of the e-petition system is that it lowers the barrier to entry — a citizen does not need to be a member of a political party, know an MP personally, or have financial resources to trigger a parliamentary response.

Social Media and Political Engagement

Social media platforms have transformed how political campaigns are run and how citizens find out about public affairs. Platforms enable citizens to share news, organise events, contact politicians directly and mobilise support for causes in ways that were not possible before the internet. Online campaigning can reach millions of people at very low cost.

Supporters of digital engagement argue that it has made politics more accessible. Young people, disabled citizens and those in rural areas — groups who historically faced barriers to participation — can now engage with public affairs from home. Campaigns focused on local issues such as saving a community library or improving pedestrian crossings can mobilise residents who might never have attended a council meeting.

Critics raise several concerns about digital democracy. First, the digital divide means that elderly citizens, those in poverty and people in areas with poor internet connectivity are less likely to participate in digital forms of civic engagement. If e-petitions and online campaigns become the dominant route to political influence, the voices of these groups may be further marginalised.

Second, critics point to “slacktivism” — where signing an online petition or sharing a social media post feels like meaningful action but produces little real-world change. One viewpoint holds that digital participation can substitute for deeper civic engagement such as joining a political party, attending public meetings or volunteering. Another viewpoint is that even low-effort digital actions build political confidence and can be a gateway to more sustained participation.

Third, social media algorithms can create “filter bubbles”, where citizens mainly see content that confirms their existing views. This can make it harder to encounter different perspectives and may deepen political polarisation rather than foster the deliberate, balanced debate that democracy requires.

Other Digital Tools for Civic Participation

Beyond e-petitions and social media, citizens have access to a range of digital tools to engage with their representatives. Most MPs and local councillors maintain email addresses and social media accounts, making it easier than ever to contact them directly. Websites such as WriteToThem.com allow citizens to locate their representatives and send messages with just a postcode. Many local councils now live-stream their meetings and publish minutes online, increasing accountability and access.

Key Fact

Key digital participation tools include: e-petitions (Parliament website), direct contact with MPs by email or social media, online council meeting access, and crowdfunding platforms for community campaigns. Each provides a different route for citizens to make their voice heard without traditional face-to-face engagement.

Voting and Digital Technology

Some commentators and politicians have proposed extending digital technology to the act of voting itself, through e-voting. Supporters argue it could increase voter turnout by making voting more convenient, especially for young voters, shift workers, and people with mobility difficulties.

Critics warn that e-voting raises serious concerns about cybersecurity, the risk of electoral fraud and the potential loss of the secret ballot. The UK Electoral Commission has conducted trials of online voting in local elections, but no national e-voting system has been introduced. The debate continues, with one viewpoint emphasising the need to modernise democracy and another stressing the importance of proven, secure systems that citizens can trust.

A common error in exam answers is to treat all digital actions as equally meaningful forms of political participation. Examiners reward candidates who can distinguish between depth of participation. Signing an e-petition takes seconds and may or may not lead to change; joining a formal citizens’ assembly, attending a council scrutiny meeting or sustained volunteering represents much deeper engagement. When you are asked to “evaluate” digital democracy, always weigh the benefits of wider reach against the risk that shallow online actions replace deeper civic involvement.

What Is Migration?

Migration is the movement of people from one place to another. It can be internal — within a country, such as people moving from rural areas to cities — or international, meaning movement across national borders. Immigrants are people who move into a country, while emigrants are those who leave. The difference between the number arriving and the number leaving is called net migration. When more people arrive than leave, net migration is positive; when more leave than arrive, it is negative.

A Brief History of Migration to the UK

The UK has a long history as both a destination for migrants and a source of emigrants. In earlier centuries, waves of Huguenot refugees from France, Jewish communities fleeing persecution in Eastern Europe, and Irish workers seeking employment all contributed to the population. After the Second World War, the British government actively recruited workers from the Caribbean, South Asia and elsewhere to help rebuild the economy and staff the newly created NHS. The Windrush generation — named after the ship HMT Empire Windrush, which arrived at Tilbury in 1948 — became a defining part of British multicultural history.

From the 1990s onwards, migration from European Union member states increased significantly, particularly after 2004 when eight Eastern European countries joined the EU and their citizens gained the right to live and work in the UK under EU free movement rules. The UK left the EU in January 2020. Freedom of movement ended on 31 December 2020, and the points-based immigration system began on 1 January 2021 for EU citizens moving to the UK.

Key Fact

The UK left the EU in January 2020. Freedom of movement ended on 31 December 2020, and the points-based immigration system began on 1 January 2021.

Why Do People Migrate?

Geographers and social scientists use the terms “push factors” and “pull factors” to explain why people move. Push factors are conditions that make people want to leave a place — for example, conflict, poverty, political persecution, environmental disasters or lack of employment. Pull factors are conditions that attract people to a particular destination — such as higher wages, political safety, better public services, an established community of people from the same background, or family connections.

It is important to distinguish between voluntary migration (people who choose to move, typically for economic or personal reasons) and forced migration. A refugee is someone who has been forced to flee their country because of a well-founded fear of persecution on grounds such as race, religion, nationality, political opinion or membership of a particular social group. An asylum seeker is someone who has applied for refugee status but whose application has not yet been decided. Asylum seekers are not the same as illegal immigrants; the right to seek asylum is recognised in Article 14 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and the 1951 UN Refugee Convention defines who counts as a refugee and the protection they must be given.

Key Fact

A refugee has been granted protection after fleeing persecution. An asylum seeker has applied for refugee status and is awaiting a decision. Applying for asylum is a legal right under the 1951 UN Refugee Convention.

Supporters of immigration argue that it brings significant economic, cultural and social benefits. Economically, migrants often fill skills shortages in key sectors: the NHS, social care, construction and agriculture all rely substantially on migrant workers. Many economists argue that migrants contribute more in taxes and public spending than they receive in services, particularly in their working years. Culturally, immigration has enriched British food, music, art, science and sport. Demographically, immigration helps offset an ageing population by bringing in younger workers who support public pension and healthcare systems.

Critics of high levels of immigration argue that rapid population change can put pressure on public services such as schools, housing and GP surgeries, particularly in areas that receive the highest concentration of new arrivals. Some argue that unchecked immigration can suppress wages for low-paid workers in sectors where labour supply is abundant. Others raise concerns about integration: if migration is very rapid, they argue, it can be harder for communities to build the shared understanding and civic ties that make a diverse society function well. These concerns apply particularly to debates about policy, not to individuals or communities themselves. Examiners expect students to present both perspectives without dismissing either.

The Impact of Migration on UK Communities

Migration has shaped and continues to shape the UK in visible ways. Many areas of the UK have substantial communities with heritage from South Asia, the Caribbean, West Africa, Eastern Europe and the Middle East. These communities have built places of worship, businesses, cultural organisations and community networks that are part of local life. Languages, foods and festivals that originated elsewhere are now part of everyday British culture.

At the same time, migration has also raised questions about housing, labour markets and public services in specific areas. Local authorities in areas of high migration have at times reported pressure on school places, social housing and healthcare. These are policy and resource questions, not inherent consequences of migration itself — they reflect whether government investment in public services has kept pace with population growth.

Students sometimes use the terms “refugee,” “asylum seeker” and “economic migrant” interchangeably. These are legally distinct categories with different rights and obligations. An economic migrant moves voluntarily in search of better living standards. An asylum seeker is seeking legal protection because they claim to have fled persecution — their claim is assessed under international law. A refugee is someone whose claim has been accepted. Mixing up these terms in exam answers is penalised because it shows imprecise use of citizenship terminology. Use the correct term for the group you are discussing.

Migration and Citizenship Values

Questions about migration sit at the intersection of several core citizenship values: human rights (including the right to seek asylum), national sovereignty (the right of a democratic state to control its own borders), equality (treating all people with dignity regardless of their origins) and social cohesion (building a shared civic society). How to balance these values is one of the most contested political debates in contemporary democracies. As a citizenship student, your task is to understand the different perspectives, use the correct terminology and present a balanced argument — not to take a personal political position.
